messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Six years ago, Arjun, a sixty-one-year-old South Asian American paramedic, responded to a collapsed textile warehouse where drummed industrial solvents had ruptured during a structural collapse. He had descended into the unlit basement to rescue a trapped foreman, but the heavy rubber of his facepiece had split under shifting rubble. A thick, acrid vapor seeped into his airway, coating his lips with a sharp, solvent-like odor that lingered long after he was pulled to safety. In the months that followed, the memory of that exposure did not fade as he had expected. When he returned to his fire station, the workplace setting acted as a direct catalyst, instantly pulling the full memory forward. Without warning, the terror he felt during the collapse rushed back with the same visceral intensity, flooding his chest and forcing him to stop breathing as the overwhelming emotion hit him like a physical wall. Once that initial intrusion took hold, environmental cues consistently pushed him toward his only known coping mechanisms. Arjun found that walking into a darkened stairwell or stepping into a dimly lit break room would instantly trigger the full memory, the lack of light mirroring the collapsed structure. When the olfactory cue of alcohol caught his nose—whether from a coworker’s post-shift drink or a passing parade float—it crossed straight into memory, bypassing any filter and leaving him gasping as the old panic returned. Rather than letting the recall pass, he immediately retreated into rumination, his mind fixating on the exact split seconds where he might have prevented the exposure, replaying the rescue protocol until he convinced himself that different choices would have changed the outcome. To outrun the spiraling thoughts, he began keeping himself constantly surrounded by people, refusing to sit alone in his own kitchen or stand in an empty garage, because any moment of quiet let the memory surge back unbidden. This cycle cemented itself as the memory’s emotional weight dictated his daily behavior. Every time the terror on recall peaked, Arjun felt his body preparing to shut down, so he instinctively avoided medical cues, steering his own vehicle away from hospitals and ambulances, and flinching when his wife attempted to examine his skin for lingering discoloration. The absence of clinical reassurance guaranteed the memory would never settle, as his brain treated each unverified threat as a fresh near-miss. He had come to believe that his own body was betraying him, which is why he avoided medical cues entirely. This constant avoidance also sharpened his sensitivity to the original triggers; without professional grounding, routine workplace interactions and darkened corridors now felt infinitely more hazardous than they were. His nervous system remained locked in threat detection, meaning that even the faintest whiff of alcohol would strike with renewed immediacy, reinforcing the terror that he was still in danger. As the months accumulated, his strategies only deepened the loop. The constant socialising forced him to remain hyper-vigilant at the station, scanning every colleague and doorway, which meant that even routine workplace dispatches now sparked the memory of the chemical leak. His avoidance of medical settings left him physically untethered; minor skin irritation would spiral into full panic, making the workplace feel like a minefield. Now, at sixty-one, Arjun sits in a quiet clinic for the first time, his hands clasped tightly over his knees. He is here because the constant socialising has fractured his marriage, and because the overwhelm on recall no longer stays confined to the past. He hopes someone can help him stop the cycle, but his greatest fear remains that speaking about the warehouse will permanently trap him back inside the dark, choking vapor, leaving him with no escape.
